overview.title: 📖 Overview: Collusion, Guarantors, and What Cannot Be Repossessed
overview.subtitle: Arakhin 23a–23b
overview.hebrewSource: הַמַּקְדִּישׁ נְכָסָיו וְהָיְתָה עָלָיו כְּתוּבַּת אִשָּׁה, רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר אוֹמֵר: כְּשֶׁיְּגָרְשֶׁנָּה יִדּוֹר הֲנָאָה
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: A new mishna imagines a person who consecrates all his property while still owing his wife her marriage contract (ketubah). Since the ketubah debt is secured by his property, she could, after a divorce, collect it out of the consecrated funds — and then quietly remarry him, having together extracted value from the Temple treasury. Rabbi Eliezer worries about exactly this scheme; Rabbi Yehoshua does not. The Gemara probes the dispute's real basis through several reinterpretations, tells a story about a guarantor's son caught in the same bind, and then turns to two further mishnayot: how the Temple redeems consecrated property burdened by debts, and — crucially — what basic possessions the treasury may never take from a debtor, even one who owes valuations.

slides.title: 🤝 The Collusion Vow: Necessary or Not?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua, extended by Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel to guarantors

lines.speaker: R' Eliezer
lines.text: One who consecrates his property while owing his wife her ketubah must, upon divorcing her, vow that benefit from her is forbidden to him — otherwise she collects from the Temple's funds and he quietly remarries her.

lines.speaker: Rabban Shim'on b. Gamliel
lines.text: The same concern applies to a guarantor of a woman's ketubah: if her husband divorces her and cannot pay, he too must vow benefit from her forbidden, lest they collude against the guarantor's property and then remarry.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: What's the root of the Eliezer/Yehoshua dispute? R' Eliezer holds a person would scheme against Temple property; R' Yehoshua holds he would not.

slides.title: 🕵️ Testing the Dispute's Real Basis
slides.subtitle: The Gemara tries several explanations before settling on one

nodes.content: ❓ Rav Huna: a dying man's claim 'I owe so-and-so 100 dinars' is believed even after consecrating everything — 'a person does not collude against hekdesh.' Doesn't this contradict Rabbi Eliezer?
💡 Attempt 1: the dispute is only about a healthy person; all agree a dying person gains nothing personally, so he would never lie ('a person sins only for his own benefit')

columns.label: Attempt 2
columns.content: Both agree collusion is a real concern; they disagree only whether a public vow can later be nullified

columns.label: Final answer
columns.content: They disagree whether a vow can be dissolved when it concerns consecrated property — R' Eliezer says no, so the vow truly blocks collusion

nodes.content: 📜 Support: Rabbi Elazar b. Rabbi Shimon links this exactly to Beit Shammai (mistaken consecration is still valid) vs. Beit Hillel (it is not, so it can be dissolved)

slides.title: 😔 The Case of Moshe bar Atzrei's Guarantee
slides.subtitle: A real-world test of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling

steps.content: 1️⃣ Moshe bar Atzrei guaranteed his daughter-in-law's ketubah; his son Rav Huna, a struggling Torah scholar, needed money
2️⃣ Abaye: let someone advise Rav Huna to divorce his wife, have her collect her ketubah from his father the guarantor, then remarry her — netting the family cash
3️⃣ Rava objects: but the mishna requires the collusion-vow first, which would bar remarriage! Abaye: divorce outside court, and no vow is administered
4️⃣ It later emerged Rav Huna was a priest — forbidden to remarry a divorcée regardless. Abaye: 'poverty follows the poor'

callout.label: Legal footnote:
callout.text: The scheme only worked because Moshe bar Atzrei was a kablan (one who accepts unconditional guarantor responsibility) rather than an ordinary arev — the halakha ultimately follows that a guarantor is liable even if the debtor has no property, except an ordinary guarantor of a ketubah, since he 'performs a mitzva' and loses nothing himself.

slides.title: 💵 New Mishna: Redeeming Property Owed to Both a Wife and a Creditor
slides.subtitle: Neither collects directly from the Temple treasury
rows: Neither the wife nor the creditor collects straight from hekdesh
The one who redeems must redeem the property first, then pay them
Why redeem at all, instead of transferring directly?
So people won't say 'consecrated property leaves sanctity without redemption'
Property worth 9,000 dinars consecrated, debt is 10,000 — creditor lends one more dinar so the debtor can 'redeem' the property for a token sum
This cheap-redemption method works only if the debt roughly matches the property's value
The consecrated property must be worth at least half the debt

slides.title: 🎒 What the Treasury Must — and Must Not — Leave Behind
slides.subtitle: A valuations-debtor keeps basic necessities; someone who consecrates ALL his property does not

boxes.title: Kept by an Arakhin Debtor
items: Food for 30 days, clothing for 12 months
A made bed, sandals, and tefillin (Lev. 27:8, 'sustain him')
Two tools of his craft; R' Eliezer: a farmer keeps his plow-team, a donkey-driver his donkey
If he has many of one tool and few of another, none are sold to balance it out

boxes.title: Taken from One Who Consecrates ALL His Property
items: Even his tefillin — since he declared 'all my property,' nothing is excluded
The Rabbis hold plow-oxen and a donkey are not 'craft tools' but ordinary property, so they too are taken

callout.label: But never his family's:
callout.text: The mishna is explicit that basic provisions are never left for his wife or children — only for the debtor himself, per the verse's own wording, 'sustain him.'

summary.principle: The court requires a divorcing husband with consecrated property to vow away benefit from his ex-wife only where genuine concern for collusion against an irreversible consecration exists; and while the Temple treasury may repossess property for unpaid valuations, it must leave the debtor basic sustenance, tools, and dignity — though one who consecrates absolutely everything forfeits even that.

flowSteps.content: 🤝 R' Eliezer requires an anti-collusion vow after divorce; R' Yehoshua does not; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel extends it to guarantors
🕵️ The Gemara narrows the dispute: it's about whether a vow on consecrated property can ever be dissolved

columns.content: 😔 Moshe bar Atzrei's case shows the scheme fails when the son turns out to be a kohen
💵 Debts on consecrated property are paid via cheap redemption, never direct transfer

flowSteps.content: 🎒 Even a debtor stripped of property for arakhin keeps food, clothes, a bed, and his trade tools — but all-property consecration takes even tefillin
🎓 Key Principle: Jewish law guards against real collusion but also guards a debtor's basic human dignity, drawing the line precisely at what the Torah's own words support

quiz.q: Why does Rabbi Eliezer require a man who consecrated his property and then divorces his wife to vow that benefit from her is forbidden to him?
o: To punish him for consecrating his property
To prevent collusion: she could collect her ketubah from the consecrated property, and then he could remarry her, effectively recovering Temple funds for the family
Because Jewish law always requires such a vow after any divorce
To ensure she never remarries
quiz.e: Rabbi Eliezer is concerned about a scheme where the divorced wife collects her ketubah debt from the consecrated property and the couple then remarries, having effectively extracted Temple treasury funds for themselves.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara ultimately explain the basis of the Rabbi Eliezer/Rabbi Yehoshua dispute?
o: They disagree about whether ketubah debts are valid at all
They disagree about whether a vow made regarding consecrated property can later be dissolved (annulled) by a halakhic authority
They disagree about the value of the consecrated property
They disagree about whether women may collect ketubah payments
quiz.e: The Gemara settles on explaining that Rabbi Eliezer holds a vow concerning consecrated property cannot be dissolved (so the anti-collusion vow is truly effective), while Rabbi Yehoshua holds it can be dissolved, making the vow pointless as a safeguard.

quiz.q: What was revealed about Rav Huna (son of the guarantor Moshe bar Atzrei) that undermined Abaye's proposed scheme for him to gain money?
o: He had no wife to divorce
He was discovered to be a priest (kohen), who is forbidden to remarry a woman he divorced
He had already paid off the debt
He was not actually a Torah scholar
quiz.e: It emerged that Rav Huna was a kohen, who by Torah law may never remarry a woman he divorced — making Abaye's divorce-and-remarry scheme impossible, prompting Abaye's remark 'poverty follows the poor.'

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Abbahu, why does the mishna require that consecrated property burdened by debts be formally 'redeemed' rather than simply handed over to the creditor or wife?
o: Redemption always yields a higher price for the Temple
So that people should not say that consecrated property left its sacred status without any redemption
Because direct transfer is halakhically impossible for any consecrated item
Because the creditor prefers cash to property
quiz.e: Rabbi Abbahu explains the requirement to formally redeem the property is to avoid the appearance (and reality) that hekdesh property exited consecration without a proper act of redemption.

quiz.q: What is left for a debtor whose property is repossessed for an unpaid valuation (arakhin), according to the mishna, and how does this differ from someone who consecrates ALL his property?
o: Both cases leave the debtor with nothing at all
The arakhin debtor keeps food for 30 days, clothing for a year, a bed, sandals, and tefillin; but one who consecrated everything has even his tefillin taken
The arakhin debtor loses his tefillin but keeps everything else
There is no difference between the two cases
quiz.e: The mishna leaves an arakhin debtor basic sustenance items including tefillin, based on the verse 'sustain him.' But someone who explicitly consecrated 'all his property' has even his tefillin taken, since his declaration excluded nothing.
